title: Child in New York dies after contracting measles, governor says
content: A child in Lewis County, New York, has died after contracting measles, Gov. Kathy Hochul said in a statement Monday. It is the state’s first measles-related death in 30 years. “As a mother and grandmother, I cannot imagine what this family is going through. My heart goes out to everyone who knew and loved this child,” she said. “Measles is highly contagious, and vaccination remains our best protection against this dangerous disease. This is New York’s first measles-related death in 30 years, a devastating reminder of what’s at stake when Washington deliberately erodes decades of progress in protecting Americans from preventable illnesses. “In New York, we will continue to stand by proven public health measures and do everything we can to keep New Yorkers safe and healthy.” CNN has reached out to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the New York state health department and the Lewis County health department for more information. Surging measles cases prompted Hochul to declare a statewide disaster emergency last month. As of Wednesday, 168 cases had been reported across New York, according to data from the CDC. Lewis County reported 15 cases as of October 14, all in people who had not received the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine. Measles typically causes about 1 in 5 people who aren’t vaccinated to be hospitalized, according to the CDC . As many as 1 out of every 20 children with measles gets pneumonia, the most common cause of death from measles in young children. One of every 1,000 kids with measles will develop encephalitis, or brain swelling. More than 4,800 measles cases have been reported across the US this year, according to the CDC – the most since 1990, a decade before measles was declared eliminated in the US. More than a quarter of those cases have been in Pennsylvania, which has reported five measles-related deaths. The Pan American Health Organization, an arm of the World Health Organization, is set to hold a measles elimination commission meeting next week, when the US is widely expected to lose the elimination status it has held since 2000. Public health experts have largely attributed the rise in measles cases in the US to falling vaccination rates , although rising cases have driven a surge of immunizations in some places. Two doses of the MMR vaccine are recommended in childhood to provide 97% protection against measles infections. In 2024, 93% of US 3-year-olds had received at least one MMR dose, according to data from the CDC’s National Immunization Surveys, below the 95% threshold needed to prevent outbreaks of the highly contagious disease. But in 2025 — a year marked by the nation’s first measles deaths in decades — the level rose to 97% among 3-year-olds. US Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has drawn broad criticism for his response to measles outbreaks, including downplaying the immunity provided by the MMR vaccine. In Pennsylvania, the measles-related deaths have also sparked a war of words between Kennedy and state officials. President Donald Trump has also repeated misinformation about vaccines, including linking them with autism and saying that children have “a tremendous amount of vaccines” put in their bodies. CNN’s Deidre McPhillips and Meg Tirrell contributed to this report.

title: The people who only need four hours' sleep
content:
Some people really are fine with remarkably little sleep. But it can be hard to tell if you're one of those people.
For as long as she can remember, Aimee Pugh Bernard hasn't needed much sleep. Today she tends to go to bed around 22:00 and wake up around 04:30. "I'm wide awake. I cannot stay in bed," she says.
Sometimes Bernard, an immunology professor at the University of Colorado, can't fall asleep right away. Then she'll log only five hours' slumber.
Perhaps most surprisingly, Bernard usually still feels energised the next day. She'll walk her dog, sweat through an hour-long gym session, and clock 1.5 hours of work before 08:00. Friends gawk at Bernard's ability to do so much on so little sleep. But in her family, it's normal – her father and brother are the same.
Most of us, of course, require more. The average adult aged 26-64 years needs about seven to nine hours of sleep in every 24 , according to the US National Sleep Foundation's latest review of the evidence.
Why there is such a wide variation in how much sleep people need has been a long-standing mystery. Yet over the last few years, scientists have pinpointed a wealth of ways in which genetics play a role. From the rare mutations carried by people like Bernard, to hundreds of much more common variants, here's why some people get away with very little sleep. In the future, these findings could be used to help protect those who can't get enough from some of the usual consequences.
In 2019, Bernard learned the likely reason for her own sleep superpower.
A research team from the University of California, San Francisco had discovered a genetic mutation related to sleep duration in humans. Although the people who carried it went to bed at fairly conventional times, they woke up very early, often getting anywhere from four to six-and-a-half hours' sleep a night. After sending a blood sample to the research team, Bernard found out that she was one of them.
This rare, heritable condition is called familial natural short sleep (FNSS). In the years since, several other mutations associated with FNSS have been identified .
One of the biggest mysteries about FNSS is that those who have it seem "fine" on so little sleep, says the team's lead investigator, molecular biologist Ying-Hui Fu. Exactly why is still being worked out.
There is intriguing evidence that FNSS-linked genetic variations might not only cause short sleep but protect those who have it from the consequences. This includes memory impairment, for example.
One 2019 experiment led by Fu introduced a mutation linked to FNSS in mice. The team found that the mice with a related variant not only slept less, but seemed to be protected from memory deficits . Another test found that mice with some of these variants were less likely to develop a mouse version of Alzheimer's.
In 2014, an international research team investigated a pair of human fraternal twins where one twin had a short-sleep mutation and the other did not. They found that the carrier twin regularly slept about an hour less than their sibling. They also discovered that when both twins were kept continuously awake for 38 hours, the carrier twin had about 40% fewer performance lapses than the other twin.
The researchers also found some intriguing differences between how the two twins slept. Even though the carrier twin slept less, he had almost the same amount of non-REM sleep as his brother. This includes slow-wave or "deep" sleep, which could mean that he was, in some ways, getting more benefits from the sleep he did obtain.
Still, research in the area is ongoing – and critical, says Fu.
Over the last few years, there has been increasing interest in how our understanding of these genetic variations could be harnessed to help people. Within the pharmaceutical industry, there are hopes that one day discoveries about short sleepers could lead to drugs for treating sleep disorders or help military personnel to get by on less sleep, for example.
For that, scientists not only need a clear idea of whether the variants protect short sleepers from negative consequences, but also exactly how they do so. Without this information, you could wind up creating a drug with unexpected side effects. "You have to understand how it works," says Fu. "You don't want to sleep less and then get Alzheimer's or Parkinson's or cancer after 10 years, or five years, or 20 years."
While the genetic mutations associated with FNSS are one of the more extreme and exciting examples, they are only a handful of those that can shape our sleep duration.
Overall, how long we sleep for is estimated to be anywhere from 30 to 65% heritable , meaning that up to 65% of the difference in sleep duration between us can be explained by genetics. So far, several hundred different parts of the genome have been identified as influencing sleep duration. In one new analysis that looked at data from nearly 650,000 adults, there were around 244. (The research has not yet been published and is currently in preprint .)
If you took any single one of these common mutations on its own, it would only be linked to a difference in sleep duration of about a minute, says the paper's lead author, geneticist Isabelle Austin-Zimmerman at King's College London.
ranking_reason: A new scientific discovery about genetic variations influencing sleep duration, with potential applications in treating sleep disorders or improving military personnel's sleep habits.
